title: Data Science Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Data Science lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Begin with a clear question
entries.summary: Data is recorded information. Data science uses careful questions and checks to learn from it. A clear question tells us what we need to count.

example.code:
Question: which book type was borrowed most this week?
Needed: one row per borrowing and the book type
Not needed: learner names or home addresses
Result: a count for each type

notes: Collecting extra personal details does not make an answer better.

entries.name: Organise rows and columns
entries.summary: A row holds one record. A column holds one kind of information. A list of dictionaries can represent a small table in Python.
notes: Use the same meaning and unit for a column in every row.

entries.name: Read a tiny CSV table
entries.summary: CSV stores table rows as text, often with commas between fields. A CSV reader handles fields more carefully than splitting every line yourself.

example.code:
import csv
from io import StringIO
text = "type,count\nstory,4\nscience,2\n"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(StringIO(text)))
print(rows[0]["count"])

notes: A value read from CSV is not automatically a number.

entries.name: Use consistent units
entries.summary: Before comparing measurements, put them in the same units. Metres and centimetres describe length on different scales.

example.code:
lengths_cm = [100, 150, 200]
lengths_m = [value / 100 for value in lengths_cm]
print(lengths_m)

notes: Adding 1 metre and 50 centimetres as if they were both the same unit gives a wrong result.

entries.name: Handle missing values honestly
entries.summary: A missing value means a measurement is absent. It does not mean zero. Keep track of what you leave out of a calculation.

example.code:
minutes = [10, None, 20]
known = [value for value in minutes if value is not None]
print(sum(known) / len(known), len(known))

notes: If no values are known, check before dividing by the list length.

entries.name: Check duplicate records
entries.summary: A duplicate is a repeated record. Some repeats are mistakes, but repeated events can also be real. Use a suitable identifier before removing anything.

example.code:
events = [{"id": "a", "type": "story"}, {"id": "a", "type": "story"}, {"id": "b", "type": "story"}]
ids = [row["id"] for row in events]
print(len(ids), len(set(ids)))

notes: Do not remove all repeated values when separate events can share them.

entries.name: Count categories
entries.summary: A category is a named group. Counter counts how often each value occurs in a list.

example.code:
from collections import Counter
borrowings = ["story", "science", "story", "poetry"]
counts = Counter(borrowings)
print(counts["story"], counts["science"])

notes: Always say what a count refers to: books, events and people are different things.

entries.name: Mean and median show different centres
entries.summary: The mean adds values and divides by their count. The median is the middle value after sorting. A very large value can pull the mean upward.

example.code:
from statistics import mean, median
minutes = [2, 3, 4, 5, 36]
print(mean(minutes), median(minutes))

notes: Do not report an average without checking how spread out the values are.

entries.name: Look at spread
entries.summary: Spread describes how far apart values are. The range subtracts the smallest value from the largest. It is a simple start, not a full description.
notes: Two lists can have the same range and very different middle values.

entries.name: Choose a clear chart
entries.summary: A chart should fit the question. Bars compare category counts. A line can show ordered measurements over time. Labels must name the values and units.

example.code:
Question: compare borrowings by book type
Chart: bars
Horizontal labels: story, science, poetry
Vertical label: number of borrowings
Bar baseline: zero

notes: A chart with missing units or a misleading scale can suggest the wrong story.

entries.name: A pattern does not prove a cause
entries.summary: Two things can change together without one causing the other. A third factor or the way data was collected may explain the pattern.

example.code:
Observed: more ice cream sales and more swimming on hot days
Possible shared cause: warm weather
Unsupported claim: buying ice cream makes people swim

notes: Do not turn a shared pattern into a cause claim without evidence.

entries.name: Report the answer and its limits
entries.summary: A useful report states the question, result, method and limits. Readers should be able to check where the answer came from.

example.code:
Question: which type was borrowed most this week?
Sample: 4 fictional borrowing events
Result: story had 2 events; science and poetry had 1 each
Limit: one tiny week does not describe the whole year

notes: Do not hide missing data or small samples behind a confident title.
